 Starting January 1, a Donation to a Scholarship Fund Cuts Your Federal Tax Bill by Up to $1,700, Dollar for Dollar. It Only Works in States That Opted In, and Here’s the List
 Vilma Rios Thu, November 19, 2026 at 4:19 AM EST 5 min read Quick Read 
 Starting January 2027, a new federal credit returns every dollar of cash gifts to approved scholarship groups, up to $1,700 per person. 
 A retired couple in the 22% bracket who gives $1,700 saves nothing with the standard deduction, but the credit wipes out $1,700 of tax. 
 Only about 30 states opted in, but your home state doesn't matter: giving to an approved group in a listed state qualifies.

 Most charitable gifts return only a slice of what you give, and only if you itemize. Starting January 1, 2027, one kind of gift gives back every dollar, up to a cap. 
 tiero / iStock via Getty Images A new federal provision, Section 25F of the Internal Revenue Code, gives a dollar-for-dollar credit for cash donations to nonprofits that fund K-12 scholarships. The cap is $1,700 per taxpayer. The catch is location. The scholarship group has to be on the list of a state that chose to participate, and 31 states were on the IRS list as of November 13, 2026. 
 How Section 25F Turns a $1,700 Gift Into a $1,700 Tax Cut 
 Congress created the credit in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, signed into law in July 2025. The statute allows a credit equal to the qualified contributions you make during the year, capped at $1,700 under 26 U.S.C. § 25F(b)(1). 
 A deduction lowers your taxable income, so it's worth only your bracket rate. A credit comes straight off the tax you owe. Treasury and the IRS issued proposed regulations, along with companion temporary regulations, on October 1, 2026. Taxpayers may rely on the proposed regulations for contributions made on or after January 1, 2027.

 Worked Example: Credit Versus Deduction for a Retired Couple 
 Consider a hypothetical retired couple filing jointly in the 22% bracket. They take the standard deduction, which is $32,200 for couples in tax year 2026, like most retirees. 
 If they give $1,700 to their usual charity, they get no federal tax benefit because they don't itemize. Even if they did itemize, the deduction would save only $374. Give the same $1,700 to a listed scholarship group and their tax bill drops by the full $1,700. That's $1,326 more in their pocket. 
 Story Continues Under the proposed regulations, each spouse filing jointly gets a separate $1,700 limit. A couple can claim up to $3,400 if each spouse makes a big enough qualified gift.

 Which States Opted In for 2027 
 Under the law, a "covered State" is a state or D.C. that voluntarily elects to participate. Each year, it has to send the IRS its list of approved scholarship groups by January 1. As of June 8, 2026, the IRS had confirmed these states: 
 Alabama, Alaska, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Indiana, Iowa, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Virginia, West Virginia and Wyoming (27 states). 
 Later reports add Kansas, Kentucky, New Mexico and North Carolina, which brings the total to 31. 
 The list controls where the charity is located, and your own address doesn't matter. Under the proposed rules, your state of residence does not determine eligibility. A retiree in Washington, which wasn't on the list, can still claim the credit by giving to an approved group in Texas. 
 Fine Print That Can Shrink or Erase Your Credit 
 You need tax to offset. The credit is nonrefundable, so it can't create a refund. Any unused credit carries forward for up to five years. That matters for retirees who owe little federal tax. 
 A state credit cuts the federal one. Section 25F(b)(2) deducts any state credit you claim for the same gift. Under the proposed rules, the state credit comes off before the cap applies. Give $2,500, get a $500 state credit, and you still keep the full $1,700 federal credit. 
 No double dip. You can't also deduct the gift as a charitable contribution under Section 170, per § 25F(e). 
 Cash only, and it must be designated. Digital assets don't count. You have to designate the gift for Section 25F when you make it, and that choice is irrevocable. 
 No directing money to your grandchild. Scholarship groups can't earmark donations for a particular student. 
 Individuals only. Gifts made through partnerships and S corporations don't qualify under the proposed rules. 
 On the receiving end, scholarships go to students whose household income is no more than 300% of the area median. 
 Your Three Moves Before the Credit Goes Live 
 Wait for the calendar. Give on or after January 1, 2027. A December 2026 gift gets only the regular charitable deduction. 
 Check the IRS list first. You can generally rely on a group's spot on the IRS list when you give, so confirm it's there before you write the check. 
 Give in each spouse's name. Two separate gifts can double the household credit. 
 Keep an eye on the final rules. Comments on the proposed regulations close December 1, 2026, so the details could still change. If you also have a state credit or a large carryforward, it's worth running the numbers with a CPA before you give.
